claim: D1-01 (a replaced child writes after its replacement started): leases plus fencing by sequence number (Gray and Cheriton 1989; Burrows 2006), because a session cannot be relied on to stop itself, so fencing is checked at the resource.

D1-02 (a slow child cannot be told from a dead one): unreliable failure detectors and the phi accrual detector (Chandra and Toueg 1996; Hayashibara et al. 2004), using progress rather than liveness, with a hard upper bound and suspicion suspended across a PC pause.

D1-03 (crash of a child loses in-flight work and orphans helpers): checkpointing and message logging (Elnozahy et al. 2002) and atomic commit by rename (Dean and Ghemawat 2004), with piecewise determinism failing so replay is not used and the transcript serves as a write-ahead log.

D1-04 (same-model readers fail together): N-version programming (Avizienis 1985), the experimental test of independence (Knight and Leveson 1986) and data diversity (Ammann and Knight 1988), where agreement is not counted as masking and diversity comes from inputs or from a verifier of another kind.

D1-05 (a component answers wrongly and convincingly, Byzantine): the signed-message route (Lamport, Shostak and Pease 1982; Castro and Liskov 1999), not replication, because replica independence fails; a script checks quote and snapshot hash and the model step is labelled judgment.

D1-06 (where to put the correctness check across several hops): the end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed and Clark 1984), so the endpoint is the owner's page and the synthesis, one hop later than the current check.

D1-07 (costly effects must happen exactly once under retry and restart): idempotence keys (Helland 2012) and entities and activities without distributed transactions (Helland 2007), with intent written before the effect and reconciliation against the observed world after restart.

D1-08 (admission under a token budget, bounded concurrency, barrier waves): escrow (O'Neil 1986) and Little's law (Little 1961), reserving an estimate with margin and enforcing at the consumer, with waves of three treated as a barrier.

D1-09 (restart storms; local fault versus common cause): supervision trees and restart intensity (Armstrong 2003), keeping R small and escalating, since a restart costs many tokens and common cause stops admission.

D1-10 (bounding the state of a long-running coordinator): snapshotting and log compaction (Ongaro and Ousterhout 2014) and the state machine approach (Schneider 1990), split into a deterministic script and a judgment session, with only the script's output as the snapshot.

D1-11 (duplicate work across fields): coordination avoidance (Bailis et al. 2014) and a grow-only replicated set (Shapiro et al. 2011), with no withholding of a claimed paper and deduplication of the reading (cache) rather than of the use.
D1-12 (a rarely exercised recovery path is broken when needed): crash-only software (Candea and Fox 2003), since recovery is not cheap here because a fresh reviewer re-reads the pack.

D1-13 (completeness of the failure analysis): the failure semantics taxonomy of Cristian 1991 (crash, omission, timing, response, arbitrary), where the component list is the weak point and needs the fetch tool, usage meter, PC power state, owner, transcripts, git and scripts added.

D2-01 (packing questions into fields of bounded size): B+ tree layout and bulk loading at a fill factor, with expected occupancy under random growth (Bayer and McCreight 1972; Comer 1979; Yao 1978); four assumptions fail, so sample first in a pilot and load with slack.

D2-02 (a field overflows its budget): split at insert time by key, redistribution before splitting (B*-tree), out-of-line storage, and sibling links with a high key (B-link tree); here the key range is split at plan time, overflow goes to a sibling with slack, and sibling links are a one-line pointer only.

D2-03 (crash recovery of research state): ARIES write-ahead logging (Mohan et al. 1992) and transaction logging (Gray and Reuter 1993), with value logging of the after-image, never the intent, since redo by re-running a brief is not deterministic and logging makes a wrong card durable, not true.

D2-04 (cost of re-reading a growing coordinator window; hand-over): checkpoints bound redo to the log after the checkpoint (Mohan et al. 1992) and the optimum checkpoint interval (Young 1974), with the formula derived rather than borrowed, and the status made a view computed from the logs.
D2-05 (write-write conflicts, merged ledgers): shared-nothing partitioning (Stonebraker 1986), which nothing enforces except discipline, and wall-clock merge misorders across sleep.

D2-06 (duplicate work, claim or validate): optimistic concurrency control (Kung and Robinson 1981) and a unique key with atomic insert-if-absent (SQL unique constraint, exclusive create); the withdrawn register's check-then-claim reason is no reason.

D2-07 (reviews citing cards, integrity and lineage): keys and foreign keys (Codd 1970), why and where provenance (Buneman, Khanna and Tan 2001) and view maintenance (Gupta and Mumick 1995); constraints catch dangling references but not a false sentence that cites a valid card.

D2-08 (retyped numbers and conditions in redundant copies): normal forms (Codd 1970), storing each fact once and joining to present it, since copies are typed by models and retyping can drop or distort, so no denormalising by hand.

D2-09 (a source that changes or is read unfaithfully): isolation phenomena (Berenson et al. 1995) and multiversion snapshot reads (Bernstein and Goodman 1983), with the harness owning versioning by snapshot at read time, since the web keeps no versions and the fetch tool returns a summary.

D2-10 (reviewer reading unconfirmed dirty cards): schedules that avoid cascading aborts and strict schedules (Bernstein, Hadzilacos and Goodman 1987), since a window is a read set nobody tracks and cannot be undone.

D2-11 (completeness of the failure list against a catalogue): the isolation anomaly catalogue (Berenson et al. 1995) and the transaction failure catalogue (Gray and Reuter 1993), complete only for storage and concurrency, since language-model faults are Byzantine and absent from these catalogues.

D2-12 (cost estimate and admission from statistics): cost-based plan selection (Selinger et al. 1979) and mid-query re-optimisation (Kabra and DeWitt 1998); one pilot is a sample of one field, so estimate per unit and check during the run.

D2-13 (injection: source text acts as instruction): parameterised statements (OWASP guidance, original paper not recorded), which a model cannot use since it has one channel, so a filter is not trusted and free text reaching a session with tools is shrunk.

D3-01 (when to hand over a growing session): economic order quantity (square-root law, Harris 1913) and the optimum checkpoint interval (Young 1974); the formula does not price the information a hand-over loses, g is not constant, and a separate bound on hand-overs per task is kept.
D3-02 (the window as memory with no page replacement): the working set model (Denning 1968), so large objects stay out of resident memory, a reference is held, and a helper reads them.

D3-03 (too many sessions for the PC's memory, thrashing): load control by working set (Denning 1968), admitting a session only when free memory minus reserve covers the measured peak, since a fixed count of three is a static level.

D3-04 (admission under uncertain job sizes): exponential averaging of measured job lengths (Silberschatz and Galvin), with admission on a pessimistic estimate and a run-time quota, since one pilot is one sample and only a session can read the meter.

D3-05 (spend limits enforced from outside): soft and hard resource limits (POSIX getrlimit and setrlimit, IEEE Std 1003.1), with the hard limit set below the true allowance by poll plus wake latency times spend rate, since count comes from the transcript a poll later.

D3-06 (watchdog; livelock versus progress): a progress-kicked watchdog (standard embedded practice, author not read), with suspend detected as a gap between polls and every deadline shifted, since sleep stops the watcher too.
D3-07 (lost wake-up; a notify is a hint): Mesa monitor semantics (Lampson and Redell 1980), re-checking the condition after a notify, and coalescing wakes because a wake costs a full window read.

D3-08 (restart storms): supervisor restart intensity (MaxR restarts within MaxT, then escalate; Armstrong 2003), since a fault from the brief or pack is systematic and a same-model replacement repeats it.

D3-09 (recovery from durable state in a non-deterministic system): a commit record written last with atomic replace (Gray and Reuter 1993) and the optimum checkpoint interval (Young 1974), recovering only from committed outputs and never by replay, since replay assumes piecewise determinism.

D3-10 (race on a shared claim, check then act): atomic exclusive create as the lock primitive (O_CREAT with O_EXCL, Node wx) and leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989), with the claim a shared-cache entry that the child makes because readers hold no write tools.

D3-11 (speed-up from parallel children): Amdahl's law (Amdahl 1967) and the Universal Scalability Law (Gunther 2007), which are about time and not tokens, so children never lower total tokens, and with N at most 3 a fit is a reading, not a law.

D3-12 (choosing fan-out when cost grows with window squared): the cost model of D3-01 applied to partitioning, derived here from Harris 1913 and Young 1974, where fields are not equal parts, splitting cuts knowledge apart unpriced, and coordinator cost grows with k.

D3-13 (dirty state in the researcher's window at review): flush dirty lines before eviction (Smith 1982) and crash-only software (Candea and Fox 2003), since impressions that cannot be stated as cards cannot be flushed and enter a same-window review only as uncited bias.

D3-14 (order of starting fields under a budget that may be cut): Smith's rule, weighted shortest processing time (Smith 1956), with precedence constraints (the measurement field first) and aging to stop starvation, since costs are estimates.

D4-01 (how well a checker finds faults, its detection rate): error seeding (Mills 1972), mutation analysis (DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward 1978) and fault injection (Arlat et al.), since nobody knows how a model's own fabrications are distributed and hand-made mutants may be easier or harder than real errors.

D4-02 (correlated failure of same-model versions): N-version programming (Avizienis 1985) and the coincident-failure model (Eckhardt and Lee 1985), since one model gives one difficulty function with beta near 1, so apparent diversity can come from sampling noise.

D4-03 (where to put the check in a chain of hand-overs): the end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed and Clark 1984), where the endpoint is the owner and the text reaches an agent through a summary, and pages change or are PDFs.

D4-04 (defects contained within the phase that made them): design and code inspections with entry and exit criteria (Fagan 1976) and the rising cost of a defect by the phase that finds it (Boehm 1981), with a cheap check at intake and expensive judgment only where a conclusion exists.

D4-05 (completeness of the hazard list): STPA (Leveson 2011), FMEA (MIL-STD-1629A 1980), fault tree analysis (Vesely et al. 1981) and capture-recapture (Eick et al. 1992), where two same-model analysts are not independent and capture-recapture is biased low, so method diversity replaces two runs.

D4-06 (watchdog supervision of execution): a watchdog with a separate time base (IEC 61508-7 2010) and AUTOSAR logical supervision, which fails as common mode because the watcher runs on the same PC so sleep stops both, and a looping session can write new files.

D4-07 (restart from a recovery point; limit and escalate): recovery points (Randell 1975), supervision with restart intensity (Armstrong 2003) and restart curing transient but not deterministic faults (Gray 1985), so writes are atomic, checkpoints are validated, restart intensity is 1, and the input is changed as well as the session.

D4-08 (rarely exercised alternate path, fresh-session review): recovery blocks (Randell 1975) and the end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed and Clark 1984), since the alternate is an exception and so is untested when needed.

D4-09 (sampling cards to accept or reject a lot): rectifying sampling inspection (Dodge and Romig 1929) and sampling by attributes indexed by acceptance quality limit (ISO 2859-1), using a measured inspection rate d and sampling per reader, since lots are not homogeneous.

D4-10 (a correct component used outside its assumed conditions): the Ariane 501 lesson (Lions et al. 1996) and explicit context and assumption nodes in an assurance argument (Kelly 1998), with the precondition made mechanical where the vocabulary allows.

D4-11 (qualifying a verifier by known-answer tests): independent verification and validation (IEEE Std 1012), error seeding applied to a reviewer (Mills 1972) and perspective-based reading (Basili et al.); 2 to 4 plants per expert give no rate, so the rate is pooled across experts.

D4-12 (closing a dismissed lead in a hazard log): hazard tracking to closure with verification evidence (MIL-STD-882E 2012), requiring evidence for a closure and measuring the refuter by seeding, since the refuter is the same model as the reviewer.

D5-01 (unvalidated input used to build trusted data; a check after review is an audit): Clark-Wilson CDI and UDI with rule C5 and IVPs (Clark and Wilson 1987), where LLM checkers cannot be certified, only scripts can, and the derived object stays unvalidated until every input is validated.

D5-02 (confused deputy, prompt injection): capabilities instead of ambient authority (Hardy 1988) and least privilege with complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), where data and instructions share one channel so a schema check is a type check, not a taint barrier, and the child is the deputy.

D5-03 (trust labels of derived data across hand-overs): the lattice model of information flow (Denning 1976), decentralized labels (Myers and Liskov 1997) and process-granularity flow control (Krohn et al. 2007), labelling the session at the process boundary by what it read, since output depends on the whole window.

D5-04 (verification depends on a small summarising model in the attacker's channel): reference monitor and time-of-check-to-time-of-use races (Anderson 1972; Bishop and Dilger 1996), binding the check to an immutable snapshot hash, since pages change and are attacker-controlled.

D5-05 (two checkers that are not independent): separation of duty (Clark and Wilson 1987), N-version programming (Avizienis 1985) and the measured refutation of independence (Knight and Leveson 1986), with agreement never treated as independent confirmation.

D5-06 (a session that read unchecked data produces trusted output): Biba strict integrity and the low-water-mark policy (Biba 1977), with unverifiable input treated as low integrity and what the researcher read but did not write left unlabelled.

D5-07 (assurance by evidence, not self-assessment): output certification via IVPs and system logging (rule C4) (Clark and Wilson 1987), where coverage of question ids is checkable but depth is not, so the file does not claim depth.

D5-08 (the checked party must not alter its own checker): reference monitor tamper-proofness (Anderson 1972) and file integrity by hash baseline (Kim and Spafford 1994), since a child's worktree holds the schemas, check scripts and settings.

D5-09 (the coordinator reads a child's note; taint upward): Biba no-read-down applied to the most privileged subject, and privilege separation (Biba 1977; Provos and Friedl, as read), since a child's end-of-turn note is free text that can carry injected text.

D5-10 (the checker reads the attacker-controlled object it certifies): least privilege and a narrow typed interface for the verifier (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), though a page can contain text aimed at the checker and the remedy is not recorded in the text read.

D5-11 (a session writing its own audit record): secure audit logs with hash chaining (Schneier and Kelsey 1999) and logging as a system function (rule C4, Clark and Wilson 1987), where ledger lines are self-attested and token counts already come from transcripts by script.

D5-12 (integrity check at restart): re-running IVPs before a CDI is reused (Clark and Wilson 1987) and a hash baseline (Kim and Spafford 1994), where a crash can leave a half-written cards.jsonl and the remedy is not recorded in the text read.

D5-13 (enumerating threats systematically): STRIDE threat modelling per data-flow element (Kohnfelder and Garg 1999) and attack trees (Schneier 1999); since STRIDE aims at adversaries, fault classes are added as extra columns and a checked enumeration is claimed, never completeness.

D5-14 (measuring a defence's detection rate): error seeding (Mills 1972) to estimate the fraction of faults that escape detection, with seeded cards invented and subtly distorted, since seeded wrong cards may be easier to catch than natural distortions.

D6-01 (combining fallible same-model judges): the Condorcet jury theorem (Condorcet 1785) and the jury theorem with correlated votes (Ladha 1992), where independence fails badly with n_eff near 1, so rho is measured rather than assumed, and diversity comes from other sources.

D6-02 (error rate of a checker with no perfect reference): latent-class EM estimation of observer error rates (Dawid and Skene 1979) and two tests in two populations (Hui and Walter 1980; Vacek 1985), where conditional independence fails because checker and checked are one model and estimates are biased as Vacek describes.

D6-03 (accept or reject a batch of citations): acceptance sampling and rectifying inspection (Dodge and Romig 1929), the sequential probability ratio test (Wald 1945) and the exact binomial bound (Clopper and Pearson 1934), where cards of one reader share errors, so sampling is stratified by reader.

D6-04 (how many relevant sources or failure modes exist): the Lincoln-Petersen estimator (Petersen 1896; Lincoln 1930), Chapman's bias-corrected estimator (Chapman 1951) and log-linear models (Fienberg 1972), where same-model readers overlap more than chance so N is underestimated, and captures must differ in mechanism.

D6-05 (one tree run against one single-session run, noisy): two one-sided tests for equivalence (Schuirmann 1987) and McNemar's test (McNemar 1947), where one unit per arm and outputs that are not reproducible mean a difference cannot be told from noise, so the result is treated as one reading.

D6-06 (a null result taken as evidence of absence): absence of evidence is not evidence of absence (Altman and Bland 1995) and equivalence tests with a smallest effect of interest (Lakens 2017), so a lead with no informative test is untested or inconclusive, never dismissed.

D6-07 (conduct of the literature search and extraction): a protocol registered before the search (Moher et al. 2015), reporting the search (Rethlefsen et al. 2021), a flow of records with reasons for exclusion (Page et al. 2021) and double extraction (Buscemi et al. 2006), where a second extractor is not independent for same-model checkers.

D6-08 (certainty of a body of evidence): GRADE (Guyatt et al. 2008), sponsorship bias (Lundh et al. 2017) and small-study bias (Egger et al. 1997), with the domains rated qualitatively and the adaptation stated, since the formal tools assume trials on a common effect measure.
D6-09 (scoring an expert on seed questions): Cooke's classical model (Cooke 1991), where certification checks process rather than knowledge and seeds may be in training data.

D6-10 (which source of variance to replicate): generalizability theory with G-study and D-study (Cronbach et al. 1972), where a 2 by 2 design gives very wide intervals and is to be called provisional, yet still answers whether a second research run or a second reviewer buys more.
D6-11 (detecting a drop in a rate quickly): CUSUM (Page 1954), with the in-control rate unknown and not stationary, so it is estimated from the pilot in Phase I.

D6-12 (when to stop searching): the knee method and target-recall stopping in technology-assisted review (Cormack and Grossman 2016) and the capture-recapture stop (Chapman 1951; Spoor et al. 1996), using yield per question id with the D6-04 coverage estimate, since relevance is judged by a same-model reader.
D6-13 (planning cost from one pilot): internal pilot studies with re-estimation (Wittes and Brittain 1990), estimating variance at a finer unit, because one pilot field is one unit and not random.

D7-01 (trust an unreliable producer by checking a certificate): program result checking (Blum and Kannan 1995), certifying algorithms (McConnell et al. 2011), the LCF kernel (Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth 1979) and proof-carrying code (Necula 1997), where a card's semantic content is not decidable by a script, only its surface.

D7-02 (retract conclusions when a premise is withdrawn): the justification-based truth maintenance system (Doyle 1979), the assumption-based system (de Kleer 1986) and AGM belief revision (Alchourron, Gardenfors and Makinson 1985), where sessions do not record inferences, so unjustified nodes enter as assumptions labelled judgment.

D7-03 (a dismissal that must be revisited on new evidence): support-list justifications with an OUT-list in a justification-based system (Doyle 1979) and default logic (Reiter 1980), with the OUT-list written in a fixed vocabulary (approach id, measure, direction) and the semantic remainder left to the refuter.

D7-04 (results depend only on declared inputs, hermeticity): declared dependencies and rebuild correctness (Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones 2018), purely functional deployment (Dolstra et al. 2004) and dynamic dependencies recorded as discovered (Mitchell 2012), where sessions cannot be sandboxed.

D7-05 (which targets are done, stale or missing; restart without redoing): Make's timestamp-based out-of-date targets (Feldman 1979), verifying and constructive traces (Mokhov et al. 2018) and memo functions (Michie 1968), where partial outputs look complete if presence means done.

D7-06 (check the control protocol's safety and liveness over all interleavings): safety and liveness properties (Lamport 1977; Alpern and Schneider 1985) and TLA with explicit-state model checking (Lamport 1994; Holzmann 1997), where fairness fails because a sleeping PC never takes its action, so each session is abstracted to a nondeterministic choice among its fault actions.

D7-07 (prove progress): well-founded ranking or variant functions (Floyd 1967), where a session is not a program whose steps can be proved to decrease anything, so the variant is observed per time box and non-decrease is the stall signal.

D7-08 (check each translation, note to card to page): translation validation (Pnueli, Siegel and Singerman 1998; Necula 2000), where equivalence of prose is undecidable, so only structural correspondence (copied fields, numbers, ids) is checked and the rest is judgment.

D7-09 (correlated failures in redundant versions): the experimental test of independence (Knight and Leveson 1986) and result checking with certifying algorithms (Blum and Kannan 1995; McConnell et al. 2011), where a different model still shares training data, so as much of each check as possible goes into a script.

D7-10 (verify a strong untrusted prover with a weak verifier): interactive proof systems (Goldwasser, Micali and Rackoff 1985) and Arthur-Merlin games (Babai 1985), an analogy for the protocol and direct for spot-check arithmetic, since the verifier's semantic check is itself a model judgment.

D7-11 (several knowledge sources cooperating through a shared store): the Hearsay-II blackboard (Erman et al. 1980) and blackboard control (Hayes-Roth 1985), where activations cost 100,000 tokens or more and sources are unreliable, so the store is single-writer folders rather than a concurrent blackboard.

D7-12 (task allocation among agents by bids): the Contract Net Protocol (Smith 1980; Davis and Smith 1983), where every contractor is the same model and cannot estimate its own cost, so bidding carries no information here.

D7-13 (completeness of the failure list relative to a model): decomposition into safety and liveness (Alpern and Schneider 1985) and model checking with fault actions (Holzmann 1997), where no method proves a hazard list complete absolutely; completeness is relative to model, fault list and property list.

D8-01 (loss along the chain of sessions): the data processing inequality (Shannon 1948) and rate-distortion with the distortion measure fixed before compressing (Shannon 1959), where stages can add invented content, so each consumer gets a pointer to the source at depth one from every leaf.

D8-02 (end-to-end integrity of evidence): the end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed and Clark 1984) and content addressing by hash of the bytes (Merkle), where the endpoint check goes through the lossy fetch summary, so an unreachable end means unverified and no intermediate confirmation upgrades it.

D8-03 (same model, same brief, same tool fail together): N-version programming (Avizienis 1985), experimental refutation of independence (Knight and Leveson 1986) and coincident-failure models with forced diversity (Eckhardt and Lee 1985), where diversity of method, input and model is forced and the coincidence rate is measured.

D8-04 (detection power of a checker): mutation analysis (DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward 1978), where a model may spot artificial mutants, so seeded faults should mimic real faults and never leak into files a review reads.

D8-05 (free text crossing a trust boundary): language-theoretic security (Sassaman et al. 2011), be strict in what you accept (Thomson and Schinazi 2023, RFC 9413) and design by contract (Meyer 1992), where free text is an unrestricted language inside a typed record and a helper's result reaches the child's window before any script.

D8-06 (using a card outside its conditions): design by contract with the precondition at the call site (Meyer 1992), where conditions are mostly prose, so only part can be checked mechanically and the checker gets the residue.

D8-07 (research and review stages separate or fused): pipes and filters (Shaw and Garlan 1996), where the research window holds more than its pack and a fused review uses hidden, unchecked, crash-lost state, so the pipe's rate is raised with a feedback channel instead.

D8-08 (splitting work into fields with shared sources): information hiding (Parnas 1972) and cohesion and coupling (Stevens, Myers and Constantine 1974), with boundaries drawn before coupling is known, one owner per shared source and read-only users rather than a shared write.

Fan-out (D3-12): single-session tokens T1 = n*B + g*n^2/2 against a tree of k leaves; the tree wins on tokens when g*n^2*(1 - 1/k)/2 > k*H + Coord(k); a field whose window exceeds W* gets a second session from its frozen pack.
Parallel width and speed-up (D3-11): report wall-time speed-up and work ratio; if S(3) is not above S(2) plus noise, run waves of two; parallel children never lower total tokens.
Width (D1-08): admit each field when a slot is free and its escrow fits; N = 2 or 3 by free memory; a work-conserving queue instead of barrier waves.
Width by memory (D3-03): admit a session only if free memory minus reserve covers the measured peak; three is an upper bound only.
Admission estimates (D3-04 and D2-12): one pilot gives no variance; admit on a pessimistic estimate and enforce a quota.
Order (D3-14): Smith's rule, with precedence first (the measurement field), then weight over estimated cost, with aging.

Hand-over (D3-01): hand over at W* = B + sqrt(2*H*g); if W* is close to B, split the remaining work instead; stop and split at 1.5 times W*.
Coordinator hand-over (D2-04): hand over at W* computed from growth and hand-over cost; status regenerated by script from the ledgers; the successor reads protocol and status only.
Coordinator state (D1-10): hand over a snapshot from a deterministic script, not a self-written summary.
Duplicate work (D1-11): no coordination, count the overlap; an optional content-addressed card cache by exclusive create, first writer wins.
Merging (D2-05): shared-nothing partitioning with one writer per folder; ledger lines merged by wall-clock time are misordered across sleep.
Common cause (D1-09 and D3-08): two or more child failures in one window halt admission, restart nothing, and wake the coordinator.
Information hiding (D8-08): one owner for a shared source and read-only users.
Sibling talk (D8-09): the shape forbids it; cross-field question ids are each owned by one field and listed as input to the other.
Chain depth (D8-01 and D8-07): give each consumer a pointer to the source and do not fuse research and review.
Blackboard and contract net (D7-11 and D7-12): borrowed only in part; single-writer folders instead of a blackboard; bidding carries no information with same-model contractors.
Window working set (D3-02): each node's window holds only its working set; large reads go to a helper.
Hand-over loss (D8-02, D8-01 and D3-13): state not flushed as cards is uncitable, and a hand-over loses what was not written as a card.
